Heat. Energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference, flowing spontaneously from hot to cold without external work. Distinct from temperature, which measures average kinetic energy of particles, heat is the transfer process itself and is measured in joules or calories. Heat is central to thermodynamics, chemistry, and virtually all physical processes, from engine efficiency to weather to stellar fusion.

Heat is energy transferred by conduction, convection, or radiation across a temperature gradient. It always flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never reversed without work. Quantitatively, sensible heat is defined as mass times specific heat capacity times change in temperature.

Conduction is heat diffusion through matter via atomic and molecular vibrations. It occurs in solids and depends on thermal conductivity, which is high in metals and low in insulators. Convection is bulk fluid motion carrying thermal energy, dominant in liquids and gases. Natural convection is driven by density differences. Forced convection uses pumps or fans. Radiation is electromagnetic emission from matter at all temperatures and increases dramatically with temperature according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law.

The First Law of Thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy equals heat input minus work done. Heat input to a system increases internal energy or does work on surroundings. Entropy governs spontaneity. Heat flows from high to low temperature, increasing total entropy of the universe, as stated in the Second Law.

Latent heat is energy needed to change phase without changing temperature. Melting and vaporization have distinct latent heats. Specific heat capacity varies dramatically by material. Water's unusually high specific heat, roughly four-point-one-eight kilojoules per kilogram per Kelvin, makes it ideal for thermal regulation and climate moderation.

Joule showed that one calorie equals approximately four-point-one-eight-six joules, unifying heat and mechanical work and refuting the caloric fluid theory. Heat capacity varies with temperature and phase. Supercooled liquids and heated solids exhibit anomalies near phase transitions. Thermodynamics encompasses the laws governing heat transfer and energy conversion. Temperature is the driving force for heat flow, with heat being energy redistribution driven by temperature differences. Cooling is the reverse of heating and the removal of thermal energy.
